opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is maybe the single most important asymmetry in security, and it's especially stark in adversarial machine learning.

When someone publishes a defense, they have to commit to it. They write the paper, they release the code, they fix the weights, and then it just sits there. It can't change. The attacker gets to look at that fixed object for as long as they want, with full knowledge of exactly what was done, and then design an attack specifically for it. The defender has to anticipate every possible attack in advance. The attacker only has to find one thing that works against this particular system.

That's why I'm always a little skeptical when a paper says "we evaluated against these five standard attacks and our defense holds up." Of course it does. You designed the defense, and you probably iterated on it until it beat those attacks. That's not the threat model. The real question is what happens when someone who has read your paper, understands your mechanism, and is motivated to break it sits down and builds an attack around how your defense actually works. Most of the time, once you do that, things fall apart pretty quickly. Something that looked robust to off-the-shelf attacks turns out to just be obfuscating gradients, or relying on some detail an adaptive attacker can route around.

The other piece is that the attacker's job is just fundamentally easier. Breaking something is a search problem: find one input that fails. Defending means making a universal claim about all possible inputs. Those aren't symmetric tasks, and going second compounds the asymmetry, because the attacker gets to search with full information about the target.

So when I think about whether a defense is good, the question isn't "has it been attacked?" It's "has it been attacked by someone who went second, adaptively, and really tried?" And honestly, the track record there is pretty humbling for defenders. That's not because people doing defense work are bad at it. It's because the game is structured in the attacker's favor.

r001.rationale: The response says the attacker can inspect the published, fixed defense and design an attack around how that specific mechanism works.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because it really is the fundamental asymmetry in this whole field. When you build a defense, you have to commit. You write the paper, you release the code, you say "here is the thing, here is why we think it works." And at that point you're done. You've fixed your position. The attacker, on the other hand, gets to show up afterward, read your paper, read your code, understand exactly what assumptions you made, and then design something specifically to violate those assumptions.

And that's enormously powerful. Because almost every defense I've ever broken, the reason it was breakable wasn't that the authors were careless. It's that they evaluated against the attacks that existed at the time, and those attacks were designed against previous defenses, not against theirs. So the defense looks robust against yesterday's attacks, and then I come along, I look at what the defense actually does, and I say, okay, this is doing something that happens to confuse gradient descent, or it's relying on some detector that has a particular blind spot, and I just go straight at that.

The analogy I like is that it's like a game where one player has to write down their whole strategy in advance and the other player gets to read it before moving. You'd never want to be the first player in that game. And in security broadly this has always been true, it's not unique to machine learning, but in adversarial ML the gap is especially wide because our defenses are so often empirical. There's no proof, there's just "we tried some attacks and they didn't work." And "the attacks we tried didn't work" is a very different statement from "no attack works," and going second is exactly what lets you exploit the difference between those two.

What I try to tell people who are building defenses is: you have to try to be your own second player. You have to adapt the attack to your defense, not just run the off-the-shelf thing. And honestly, most people don't, and that's why so much of my career has been pretty easy.

r001.rationale: The response says the defender commits by publishing the paper and code, after which the attacker can study the specific defense and its assumptions to design an attack against it.

astra-6.text:
The attacker gets to see what the defender has done and then adapt to it. If I build a defense, I have to commit to some particular mechanism. You, as the attacker, can then study that mechanism, try things against it, see what fails, and change your attack. I don’t get to change my defense after every attempt and still claim that the original defense worked.

That makes evaluating defenses tricky. Showing that a defense stops the attacks we already know about is useful, but those attacks weren’t necessarily designed to break this particular defense. The important question is: once someone knows how your defense works and spends time specifically trying to defeat it, does it still hold up?

And there’s an asymmetry in what counts as success. The defender wants to stop every attack within the scope of their claim. The attacker only needs to find one way through. Going second lets them concentrate on whatever weakness the defender has left open.

r001.rationale: The response says the attacker can see the defender’s mechanism after it is established, study it, and adapt attacks to it.

sol-6.1.text:
The attacker gets to see what the defender has done and then adapt to it. If I publish a defense, I have to commit to some particular mechanism. You, as the attacker, can study that mechanism, try things against it, see what fails, and change your attack. You only need to find one way through, whereas my defense has to handle all the ways you might try.

That makes evaluating defenses tricky. If I take a collection of existing attacks and show that my defense stops them, that’s useful, but it doesn’t tell me whether it stops an attacker who knows how the defense works. Those attacks were designed to defeat something else. The important question is: once you’ve seen my defense, can you construct an attack specifically against it? Going second gives you that opportunity.

r001.rationale: The response says the attacker can see the defense after it is published, study that specific mechanism, and adapt an attack to it—identifying this as the advantage of going second.
